title: Walking on the water (Matthew 14:22–33)
hook: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and a hand catches him

segments.voice: Yesterday, five loaves and two fish, the Eucharist's root, and a boy's lunch fed thousands. Your line was what you hand over is enough. That same night, the disciples are out on the lake.

After the crowd is fed, Jesus sends the disciples ahead across the lake by boat, and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the water, the wind is against them, and the boat is tossed by the waves. Then, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see someone walking toward them on the water. Matthew says they were troubled and cried out in fear: it's a ghost.
screen: `A HEADWIND ALL NIGHT.` → `THE FOURTH WATCH, BEFORE DAWN.` → `SOMEONE ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Jesus speaks at once, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be of good heart: it is I, fear ye not." It is I. In Greek, two words: egō eimi, I am. At the burning bush, in the old Greek translation of Exodus, God's name for himself begins with the same two words. Some readers hear that echo here. Then Peter, being Peter, says: Lord, if it's you, tell me to come to you on the water. Jesus says one word: come. Peter climbs over the side. And he walks. On the water. Toward Jesus. Matthew is the one who tells this part. Then, the text says, Peter saw the wind was strong, and he was afraid, and he began to sink. The wind hadn't changed; it had been strong all night. What changed was where Peter was looking. As he goes under, he prays: "Lord, save me." Three words. No speech. And immediately, Matthew says, Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him. The hand was already there. Then, gently: "O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?" Little faith, not no faith. Peter got out of the boat. The others didn't. They climb in, the wind stops, and the disciples bow down and say: truly, you are the Son of God. For Catholics, Peter matters especially. He's the one they call the first pope, the rock of the Church. And here the rock is sinking. The story doesn't hide it. It shows a leader who needed catching, and a hand that caught him.
screen: `IT IS I — EGŌ EIMI.` · `COME. PETER STEPS OUT.` · `HE SAW THE WIND AND SANK.` · `IMMEDIATELY, A HAND.` · then, large: `LORD, SAVE ME.`

segments.voice: Where in your life are you looking at the wind: a money worry, a health scare, a relationship that feels like deep water? Name it plainly, inside, and notice whether you've already stepped out, already started trying. If you pray, you can say Peter's three words, Lord, save me, and picture the hand reaching out; if not, just notice where you're looking, and try looking a little further up.
egō eimi. I am, the words Jesus spoke on the water, echoing God's own name at the burning bush.
Your line: the hand is already there. Three words are enough. See you on the mountain.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass, and "Lord, save me" is used as a short prayer in hard moments; Peter's sinking and rescue is often preached as a picture of faith that falters and is caught.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 14:27, 14:30, 14:31 given from memory; confirm.
The echo of ἐγώ εἰμι with Exodus 3:14 (LXX ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν) is a common reading; confirm phrasing ('Matthew's first readers would have heard that echo').
Fourth watch (Roman reckoning) as about 3–6 a.m.: confirm.
Softened: 'Matthew's first readers would have heard that echo' became 'Many readers, then and now, hear that echo', since how strongly the phrase signals the divine name here is debated.
Peter as first pope: stated as what Catholics call him; confirm phrasing.
